lessons.title: Forces, Gravity and Resultant Forces
lessons.description: Types of forces, gravity and weight calculations, and how to find the resultant force.
lessons.content_html:
What Are Forces?

A force is a push or a pull that acts on an object. Forces are measured in newtons (N) and are vector quantities — they have both a magnitude (size) and a direction.

Forces can be contact forces or non-contact forces. Contact forces include friction, air resistance, tension, and normal contact force. Non-contact forces include gravitational, electrostatic, and magnetic forces.

Key Fact

A force is an interaction between two objects. When two objects interact, each exerts a force on the other — these are equal in size and opposite in direction (Newton’s third law).

Gravity and Weight

Gravity is a non-contact force that attracts any two objects with mass. The strength of gravity depends on the masses of the objects and the distance between them.

Weight is the force of gravity acting on an object. It depends on the mass and the gravitational field strength:

$$W = mg$$

Where \(W\) is weight in newtons, \(m\) is mass in kilograms, and \(g\) is gravitational field strength in N/kg. On Earth, \(g \approx 10\) N/kg. On the Moon, \(g \approx 1.6\) N/kg.

Mass is the amount of matter in an object, measured in kilograms. It is the same everywhere. Weight is a force and depends on the gravitational field strength at that location. An astronaut with a mass of 80 kg weighs 800 N on Earth (\(80 \times 10\)) but only 128 N on the Moon (\(80 \times 1.6\)).

Weight is measured using a Newton meter (spring balance). Mass is measured using a balance.

Resultant Forces

When multiple forces act on an object, they can be replaced by a single force that has the same effect. This is called the resultant force.

Key Fact

If forces act in the same direction, add them. If forces act in opposite directions, subtract the smaller from the larger. The resultant force acts in the direction of the larger force.

If the resultant force on an object is zero, the object is in equilibrium. This means it is either stationary or moving at a constant velocity. If the resultant force is not zero, the object will accelerate in the direction of the resultant force.

A free body diagram shows all the forces acting on a single object. Each force is drawn as an arrow starting from the object, with the length of the arrow representing the force’s magnitude and the direction showing which way it acts.

For example, a book on a table has two forces: weight acting downwards and the normal contact force acting upwards. If these are equal, the resultant force is zero and the book stays still.

When two forces do not act along the same line, you can find the resultant using a scale drawing. Draw the forces as arrows, tip-to-tail, to scale. The resultant is the arrow from the start of the first force to the end of the second. Measure its length and angle.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When a question asks about forces, always draw a free body diagram first. Label all forces clearly with their names and sizes. Remember: weight and mass are different — weight is a force (in newtons) and mass is the amount of matter (in kilograms). If the question mentions “resultant force is zero,” state that the object is in equilibrium — either stationary or at constant velocity.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Forces are vector quantities; they can be contact (friction, tension) or non-contact (gravity, magnetic)
  • Weight = mass \(\times\) gravitational field strength (\(W = mg\)); mass stays the same, weight changes with location
  • The resultant force determines motion: zero resultant means equilibrium; non-zero resultant causes acceleration

lessons.title: Work Done, Elasticity and Hooke's Law
lessons.description: Calculating work done, investigating springs with Hooke's law, and elastic potential energy.
lessons.content_html:
Work Done

When a force causes an object to move, energy is transferred. The amount of energy transferred is called the work done. Work done is calculated using:

$$W = F s$$

Where \(W\) is work done in joules (J), \(F\) is force in newtons (N), and \(s\) is the distance moved along the line of action of the force in metres (m).

Key Fact

One joule of work is done when a force of one newton moves an object one metre in the direction of the force. Work done equals energy transferred: \(W = E\).

If a force acts at right angles to the direction of motion, no work is done. For example, gravity does no work on a satellite in a circular orbit because the force is perpendicular to the direction of travel.

A box is pushed 8 m across a floor against a friction force of 25 N. Calculate the work done against friction.

\(W = Fs = 25 \times 8 = 200\) J

This 200 J is transferred to the thermal energy store of the box and floor — they warm up slightly.

Hooke’s Law

Hooke’s law states that the extension of an elastic object is directly proportional to the force applied, as long as the limit of proportionality is not exceeded.

$$F = k e$$

Where \(F\) is force in newtons, \(k\) is the spring constant in N/m, and \(e\) is the extension in metres.

Key Fact

A force-extension graph for a spring is a straight line through the origin up to the limit of proportionality. Beyond this point, the graph curves and the spring no longer returns to its original length when the force is removed — it has been permanently deformed.

Hang a spring from a clamp stand. Measure the original (natural) length. Add masses one at a time and record the new length each time. Calculate the extension by subtracting the original length from the stretched length.

Plot a force-extension graph. The gradient of the straight-line section gives the spring constant \(k\). Use a ruler with a pointer (set square) to reduce parallax error when measuring length.

Elastic Potential Energy

When a spring is stretched or compressed within its limit of proportionality, it stores elastic potential energy. This can be calculated using:

$$E_e = \frac{1}{2} k e^2$$

Where \(E_e\) is elastic potential energy in joules, \(k\) is the spring constant in N/m, and \(e\) is the extension in metres.

A spring with a spring constant of 40 N/m is stretched by 0.15 m. Calculate the elastic potential energy stored.

\(E_e = \frac{1}{2} k e^2 = \frac{1}{2} \times 40 \times 0.15^2 = \frac{1}{2} \times 40 \times 0.0225 = 0.45\) J

An object that returns to its original shape after the force is removed is called elastic. An object that is permanently deformed is said to have undergone inelastic deformation.
lessons.exam_tip_html: In Hooke’s law questions, always check units: extension must be in metres (not cm) and force in newtons. When reading a force-extension graph, the limit of proportionality is where the straight line starts to curve. The gradient of the straight section gives the spring constant \(k\).
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Work done = force \(\times\) distance (\(W = Fs\)); work done equals energy transferred
  • Hooke’s law: \(F = ke\); applies up to the limit of proportionality; force-extension graph is a straight line through the origin
  • Elastic potential energy: \(E_e = \frac{1}{2}ke^2\); stored only while the object obeys Hooke’s law

lessons.title: Speed, Velocity and Acceleration
lessons.description: Speed, velocity and acceleration equations, plus interpreting distance-time and velocity-time graphs.
lessons.content_html:
Speed and Distance

Speed is a scalar quantity — it tells you how fast something is moving but not the direction. The equation for speed is:

$$s = v t$$

Where \(s\) is distance in metres, \(v\) is speed in m/s, and \(t\) is time in seconds. This can be rearranged to \(v = \frac{s}{t}\).

Key Fact

Typical speeds: walking ~1.5 m/s, running ~3 m/s, cycling ~6 m/s, car in town ~13 m/s, car on motorway ~30 m/s, train ~55 m/s, aeroplane ~250 m/s, sound in air ~330 m/s.

Velocity

Velocity is a vector quantity. It has both magnitude (speed) and direction. An object moving in a circle at constant speed has a changing velocity because its direction is always changing.

The difference between speed and velocity matters in physics: two cars travelling at 30 m/s in opposite directions have the same speed but different velocities.

Acceleration

Acceleration is how quickly an object’s velocity changes. The equation is:

$$a = \frac{\Delta v}{t} = \frac{v - u}{t}$$

Where \(a\) is acceleration in m/s\(^2\), \(v\) is final velocity, \(u\) is initial velocity, and \(t\) is time in seconds. A negative acceleration means the object is decelerating (slowing down).

Key Fact

For uniform (constant) acceleration, use the equation: \(v^2 = u^2 + 2as\), where \(s\) is the distance travelled. This is particularly useful when time is not given in the question.

A car accelerates from 10 m/s to 30 m/s in 5 seconds. Calculate the acceleration.

\(a = \frac{v - u}{t} = \frac{30 - 10}{5} = \frac{20}{5} = 4\) m/s\(^2\)

Distance-Time Graphs

A distance-time graph shows how far an object has travelled over time. The gradient (slope) of the line gives the speed.

A horizontal line means the object is stationary. A straight diagonal line means constant speed. A curve getting steeper means the object is accelerating. The steeper the line, the faster the object is moving.

To find the speed at a specific moment on a curved distance-time graph, draw a tangent to the curve at that point. Then calculate the gradient of the tangent: \(\text{speed} = \frac{\text{change in distance}}{\text{change in time}}\).

Velocity-Time Graphs

A velocity-time graph shows how velocity changes over time. The gradient gives the acceleration. The area under the line gives the total distance travelled.

A horizontal line means constant velocity (no acceleration). A line sloping upwards means acceleration. A line sloping downwards means deceleration. The area under the graph can be found by splitting it into rectangles and triangles.

Use a dynamics trolley on a ramp with a light gate or ticker tape timer. Vary the force (by changing the mass on a pulley) while keeping the total mass constant. Measure the acceleration for each force. Plot a graph of force against acceleration — a straight line through the origin shows that \(F = ma\).
lessons.exam_tip_html: Read graph questions carefully: on a distance-time graph the gradient is speed, but on a velocity-time graph the gradient is acceleration and the area underneath is distance. If asked to “determine” a value from a curved graph, draw a tangent at the specified point and calculate the gradient of the tangent.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Speed is scalar (magnitude only); velocity is vector (magnitude and direction); acceleration = \(\frac{v - u}{t}\)
  • Distance-time graphs: gradient = speed; velocity-time graphs: gradient = acceleration, area = distance
  • For uniform acceleration without time: \(v^2 = u^2 + 2as\)

lessons.title: Newton's Laws of Motion
lessons.description: Newton's three laws of motion, inertia, F = ma calculations, and terminal velocity.
lessons.content_html:
Newton’s First Law

Newton’s first law states that an object will remain at rest or continue to move at a constant velocity unless a resultant force acts on it.

This means that if all forces on an object are balanced (resultant force = 0), the object will not change its motion. A stationary object stays still. A moving object keeps moving at the same speed in the same direction.

Key Fact

Inertia is the tendency of an object to resist a change in motion. The more mass an object has, the greater its inertia. This is why a heavy object is harder to push into motion or bring to a stop than a light one.

Newton’s Second Law

Newton’s second law states that the acceleration of an object is directly proportional to the resultant force acting on it and inversely proportional to its mass:

$$F = m a$$

Where \(F\) is the resultant force in newtons (N), \(m\) is mass in kilograms (kg), and \(a\) is acceleration in m/s\(^2\).

This tells us three things: a larger force produces a greater acceleration; a larger mass requires a greater force for the same acceleration; and if the resultant force is zero, there is no acceleration.

A 1200 kg car has a driving force of 4800 N and friction of 1200 N. Calculate the acceleration.

Step 1: Resultant force = 4800 − 1200 = 3600 N

Step 2: \(a = \frac{F}{m} = \frac{3600}{1200} = 3\) m/s\(^2\)

Newton’s Third Law

Newton’s third law states that whenever two objects interact, they exert equal and opposite forces on each other. These forces act on different objects and are always the same type of force.

Key Fact

Newton’s third law pairs always: act on two different objects, are the same size, act in opposite directions, and are the same type of force. For example, the Earth pulls you down with gravity, and you pull the Earth up with the same gravitational force.

Students often confuse balanced forces with Newton’s third law pairs. Balanced forces act on the same object (e.g. weight and normal force on a book). Newton’s third law pairs act on different objects (e.g. the book pushes the table down, the table pushes the book up).

Another misconception: “if the forces are equal and opposite, the object can’t move.” This is wrong because the two forces act on different objects. A rocket accelerates because the rocket pushes gas backwards and the gas pushes the rocket forwards — these act on different objects.

Terminal Velocity

When an object falls through a fluid (air or water), it initially accelerates due to gravity. As its speed increases, the drag force (air resistance) increases. Eventually, the drag force equals the weight and the resultant force becomes zero.

At this point, the object reaches terminal velocity — it continues to fall at a constant speed because the forces are balanced.

When a skydiver jumps, they accelerate because weight is greater than air resistance. As speed increases, air resistance increases, so acceleration decreases. At terminal velocity (~55 m/s), forces are balanced. When the parachute opens, air resistance suddenly increases above the weight, so the skydiver decelerates. A new, lower terminal velocity (~5 m/s) is reached.
lessons.exam_tip_html: The most common error in \(F = ma\) questions is forgetting to calculate the resultant force first. If driving force and friction are both given, subtract friction from the driving force to get the resultant, then use \(F = ma\). For Newton’s third law, always identify the two objects and state that the forces are equal in size, opposite in direction, and act on different objects.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • First law: no resultant force means no change in motion; inertia resists changes in velocity

lessons.title: Stopping Distances, Braking and Momentum
lessons.description: Covers what are stopping distances?, braking forces and energy, understanding momentum and more.
lessons.content_html:
What Are Stopping Distances?

When a vehicle needs to stop, it doesn't happen instantly. The stopping distance is made up of two parts: thinking distance and braking distance.

Key Fact

Stopping distance = thinking distance + braking distance

The thinking distance is how far the car travels while the driver reacts to a hazard. During this time, the vehicle continues at constant speed.

The braking distance is how far the car travels while the brakes are being applied and the vehicle is decelerating.

Several factors can increase thinking distance:

  • Tiredness or fatigue reduces reaction speed
  • Drugs and alcohol slow down the nervous system
  • Distractions like mobile phones delay reactions
  • Higher speeds mean more distance covered during reaction time

Braking Forces and Energy

When brakes are applied, friction between the brake pads and wheels creates a force that opposes motion. This braking force does work against the vehicle's kinetic energy.

The work done by braking forces transfers the vehicle's kinetic energy into heat energy at the brakes. We can calculate this using:

$$\text{Work done by brakes} = \text{Braking force} \times \text{Braking distance}$$

This work done equals the kinetic energy that was lost: \(\frac{1}{2}mv^2\)

Key Fact

Braking distance is proportional to the square of speed. Double the speed means four times the braking distance.

Braking distance increases when:

  • Vehicle speed is higher — kinetic energy increases with speed squared
  • Vehicle mass is greater — more kinetic energy to remove
  • Road conditions are poor — wet or icy roads reduce friction
  • Brake or tyre condition is poor — worn components reduce braking force

Understanding Momentum

Every moving object has momentum. Momentum is calculated using:

$$\text{momentum} = \text{mass} \times \text{velocity}$$

$$p = m \times v$$

Momentum is measured in kg⋅m/s and is a vector quantity — it has both size and direction.

In any collision or explosion, the total momentum before equals the total momentum after. This is the conservation of momentum.

For two objects colliding:

$$m_1u_1 + m_2u_2 = m_1v_1 + m_2v_2$$

Where \(u\) represents initial velocities and \(v\) represents final velocities.

Vehicle Safety Features

Modern vehicles use momentum principles to improve safety during collisions. The key is to increase the time over which momentum changes occur.

Using \(F = \frac{\Delta p}{\Delta t}\), we can see that increasing the time (\(\Delta t\)) for a momentum change reduces the force experienced.

Key Fact

Safety features work by increasing collision time, which reduces the forces acting on passengers.

Examples of safety features include:

  • Crumple zones — designed to deform and extend collision time
  • Airbags — inflate to cushion impact and increase stopping time
  • Seat belts — stretch slightly to reduce peak forces on the body
  • ABS brakes — prevent wheel locking to maintain steering control
lessons.exam_tip_html: In calculations, remember that braking distance is proportional to speed squared, not just speed. For momentum questions, always define your positive direction clearly and remember that momentum is conserved in collisions. Show your working step-by-step, especially when rearranging \(p = mv\) or using \(F = \frac{\Delta p}{\Delta t}\).
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Stopping distance combines thinking distance and braking distance, both affected by different factors
  • Braking transfers kinetic energy to heat, with braking distance proportional to speed squared
  • Momentum equals mass times velocity and is conserved in collisions
  • Vehicle safety features reduce collision forces by increasing the time over which momentum changes

lessons.title: Waves: Properties and Behaviour
lessons.description: Transverse and longitudinal waves, the wave equation, reflection, refraction and diffraction.
lessons.content_html:
What Are Waves?

Waves transfer energy from one place to another without transferring matter. The particles in the medium vibrate back and forth, but they do not travel with the wave.

There are two types of wave. In a transverse wave, the oscillations are perpendicular (at right angles) to the direction of energy transfer. Examples include light, water waves, and all electromagnetic waves.

In a longitudinal wave, the oscillations are parallel to the direction of energy transfer. Sound is the most common example. Longitudinal waves have areas of compression (particles squashed together) and rarefaction (particles spread apart).

Key Fact

All waves can be described using four properties: amplitude, wavelength, frequency, and wave speed. The wave equation links three of these: \(v = f \lambda\).

Wave Properties

Amplitude is the maximum displacement from the rest position. Larger amplitude means more energy. Wavelength (\(\lambda\)) is the distance from one point on a wave to the same point on the next wave (e.g. crest to crest).

Frequency is the number of complete waves passing a point per second, measured in hertz (Hz). The period is the time for one complete wave and is related to frequency by: \(T = \frac{1}{f}\).

The wave speed equation is:

$$v = f \lambda$$

Where \(v\) is wave speed in m/s, \(f\) is frequency in Hz, and \(\lambda\) is wavelength in metres.

A sound wave has a frequency of 440 Hz and a wavelength of 0.75 m. Calculate the wave speed.

\(v = f\lambda = 440 \times 0.75 = 330\) m/s

Reflection, Refraction and Absorption

When waves meet a boundary between different materials, they can be reflected, refracted, or absorbed. Often a combination of all three occurs.

Reflection occurs when a wave bounces off a surface. The law of reflection states that the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection (both measured from the normal).

Key Fact

Refraction occurs when a wave changes speed as it passes from one medium to another. If the wave slows down, it bends towards the normal. If it speeds up, it bends away from the normal. The frequency stays the same; only the speed and wavelength change.

Use a ripple tank to investigate reflection, refraction, and diffraction of water waves. A vibrating bar creates plane waves on the surface of shallow water. A lamp projects the wave pattern onto a screen below for observation. Vary frequency or depth to explore different wave behaviours.

For measuring the speed of sound, use two microphones a known distance apart and a data logger. Calculate speed from \(v = \frac{d}{t}\).

Diffraction

Diffraction is the spreading out of waves when they pass through a gap or around an obstacle. The effect is greatest when the gap width is about the same as the wavelength. If the gap is much larger than the wavelength, very little diffraction occurs.

Sound waves have long wavelengths (up to several metres), so they diffract easily around doors and buildings — you can hear someone around a corner. Light has very short wavelengths (around 500 nm), so it only diffracts noticeably through extremely narrow slits.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When describing refraction, always state that the wave changes speed and therefore changes direction. Remember that frequency stays the same during refraction — only speed and wavelength change. For diffraction questions, relate the gap width to the wavelength: maximum diffraction occurs when gap ≈ wavelength.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Transverse waves oscillate perpendicular to energy transfer; longitudinal waves oscillate parallel (compressions and rarefactions)
  • Wave equation: \(v = f\lambda\); period \(T = 1/f\); amplitude relates to energy
  • Waves can be reflected (angle i = angle r), refracted (speed change causes direction change), and diffracted (spreading through gaps)

lessons.title: The Electromagnetic Spectrum
lessons.description: The seven types of electromagnetic wave, their uses and dangers, and infrared emission.
lessons.content_html:
The Electromagnetic Spectrum

The electromagnetic (EM) spectrum is a continuous range of waves, all of which travel at the speed of light in a vacuum (\(3 \times 10^8\) m/s). All EM waves are transverse and can travel through a vacuum — they do not need a medium.

Key Fact

The seven types of EM wave in order of decreasing wavelength (increasing frequency) are: radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays, and gamma rays. Use the mnemonic: Running Men In Vests Usually X-ray Giraffes.

All EM waves share the same basic properties: they transfer energy, travel at \(3 \times 10^8\) m/s in a vacuum, and obey the wave equation \(v = f\lambda\). Since speed is constant, waves with higher frequency have shorter wavelength.

Uses and Dangers

Each type of EM wave has specific uses that depend on its properties.

Radio waves have the longest wavelengths and are used for television, radio broadcasts, and communication. Different wavelengths are used for different purposes — long wave can diffract around hills, while short wave can be reflected off the ionosphere for long-distance communication.

Microwaves are used in satellite communication, mobile phone signals, and microwave ovens. In ovens, microwaves cause water molecules to vibrate, heating the food.

Infrared radiation is emitted by all warm objects. It is used in remote controls, thermal imaging cameras, cooking, and optical fibre communication. Too much infrared can cause skin burns.

Visible light is the only part of the EM spectrum we can see. It is used in photography, fibre optic communication, and vision. It ranges from red (longest wavelength) to violet (shortest).

Ultraviolet (UV) causes skin to tan and is used in fluorescent lamps, security marking, and detecting forged banknotes. Overexposure causes sunburn and increases the risk of skin cancer.

X-rays can pass through soft tissue but are absorbed by bone and metal. They are used in medical imaging and airport security scanners. Overexposure can cause cell damage and cancer.

Gamma rays have the highest frequency and shortest wavelength. They are emitted by radioactive nuclei and used in cancer treatment (radiotherapy), sterilising medical equipment, and as tracers in medical imaging. They are the most penetrating and can cause serious cell damage.

Key Fact

The danger of EM radiation generally increases with frequency. Radio waves and microwaves pose low risk. UV causes sunburn and skin cancer. X-rays and gamma rays can damage cells and DNA, potentially causing cancer and mutations.

Emission and Absorption of Infrared

All objects emit and absorb infrared radiation. The hotter an object, the more infrared it emits. Dark, matt surfaces are the best emitters and absorbers of infrared. Light, shiny surfaces are the worst emitters and absorbers (they are good reflectors instead).

Fill a Leslie cube (a metal cube with four different surfaces: shiny black, matt black, shiny white, matt white) with hot water. Use an infrared detector at the same distance from each face. The matt black surface emits the most infrared; the shiny white surface emits the least.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When asked about the EM spectrum, always give specific uses for each wave type rather than vague answers. Link dangers to frequency — higher frequency waves carry more energy and cause more cell damage. If a question asks you to explain why a particular wave type is used for a specific purpose, relate it to the wave’s properties (penetrating power, wavelength, energy).
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The EM spectrum: radio, microwave, infrared, visible, UV, X-ray, gamma — all travel at \(3 \times 10^8\) m/s in a vacuum
  • Higher frequency = shorter wavelength = more energy = greater danger to living cells
  • Each wave type has specific uses linked to its properties; dark matt surfaces emit and absorb infrared best

lessons.title: Magnets, Electromagnetism and the Motor Effect
lessons.description: Permanent and induced magnets, solenoids and electromagnets, the motor effect and F = BIl.
lessons.content_html:
Permanent and Induced Magnets

A permanent magnet produces its own magnetic field. It always has a north pole and a south pole. Like poles repel; unlike poles attract. Common permanent magnets are made from iron, steel, nickel, or cobalt.

An induced magnet is a material that becomes magnetic only when placed inside a magnetic field. When removed from the field, it quickly loses its magnetism. An induced magnet is always attracted to the permanent magnet, never repelled.

Key Fact

A magnetic field is the region around a magnet where a force acts on another magnet or magnetic material. Field lines go from north to south outside the magnet. The closer together the field lines, the stronger the field.

Place a compass near a bar magnet. Mark the position of the compass needle. Move the compass so the tail of the needle is at the mark you just made. Repeat to trace a complete field line. Alternatively, place the magnet under a sheet of paper and sprinkle iron filings on top — they align with the field lines.

Electromagnetism

When a current flows through a wire, it produces a magnetic field around the wire. The field lines form concentric circles around the wire. The direction of the field can be found using the right-hand rule: point your thumb in the direction of current, and your fingers curl in the direction of the field.

A solenoid is a coil of wire. When current flows through it, the magnetic field inside is strong and uniform (like a bar magnet). The strength of the field can be increased by: increasing the current, increasing the number of turns, or placing an iron core inside the solenoid.

Key Fact

An electromagnet is a solenoid with a soft iron core. It can be switched on and off by controlling the current. This makes electromagnets useful in scrapyard cranes, circuit breakers, electric bells, and MRI scanners.

The Motor Effect

When a current-carrying wire is placed in a magnetic field, it experiences a force. This is called the motor effect. The force is at its maximum when the wire is perpendicular to the magnetic field and zero when the wire is parallel to the field.

The size of the force is given by:

$$F = BIl$$

Where \(F\) is force in newtons, \(B\) is magnetic flux density in tesla (T), \(I\) is current in amps, and \(l\) is the length of wire in the field in metres.

Fleming’s left-hand rule predicts the direction of the force. Hold your left hand with the thumb, first finger, and second finger all at right angles. The first finger points in the direction of the magnetic field (north to south), the second finger points in the direction of conventional current, and the thumb shows the direction of the force (motion).

Electric Motors

A simple d.c. motor uses the motor effect to produce rotation. A coil of wire is placed between the poles of a magnet. When current flows, one side of the coil is pushed up and the other is pushed down (by the motor effect), creating a turning force.

A split-ring commutator reverses the direction of current in the coil every half turn. Without it, the coil would rotate 180° and then stop. The commutator ensures the forces always act in the right direction to keep the coil spinning continuously.

The speed of a motor can be increased by: increasing the current, using a stronger magnet, or adding more turns to the coil.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For the motor effect, always state the equation \(F = BIl\) and use Fleming’s left-hand rule to find the direction. In questions about electromagnets, list the three ways to increase the field strength (more current, more turns, iron core). Remember that the split-ring commutator reverses the current direction every half turn to keep the motor spinning.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Permanent magnets always have north and south poles; induced magnets only work inside a magnetic field
  • A solenoid with an iron core is an electromagnet; field strength increased by more current, more turns, or an iron core
  • Motor effect: \(F = BIl\); direction found by Fleming’s left-hand rule; split-ring commutator enables continuous rotation

lessons.title: Moments, Levers, Gears and Momentum Changes
lessons.description: Calculating moments and momentum, and how levers and gears multiply forces.
lessons.content_html:
Moments and Turning Forces

A moment is the turning effect of a force around a fixed point called the pivot. The size of the moment depends on the force applied and the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action of the force:

$$M = F \times d$$

where \(M\) is the moment in newton metres (Nm), \(F\) is the force in newtons (N) and \(d\) is the perpendicular distance from the pivot in metres (m).

Key Fact

The distance must be the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action of the force — not the distance along the object itself if the force is applied at an angle.

If an object is balanced (in equilibrium), the total clockwise moment about any pivot equals the total anticlockwise moment. This is called the principle of moments.

A child weighing 400 N sits 2.0 m from the pivot of a see-saw. Where must a child weighing 500 N sit to balance it?

Clockwise moment = Anticlockwise moment

$$500 \times d = 400 \times 2.0$$

$$d = \frac{800}{500} = 1.6 \text{ m from the pivot}$$

Levers and Gears

A lever is a simple machine that uses moments to multiply forces. By applying a small force at a large distance from the pivot, a larger force can be produced at a shorter distance from the pivot on the other side. Examples include crowbars, wheelbarrows and scissors.

The longer the lever arm (distance from effort to pivot), the less force is needed to produce the same turning moment. This is why a long spanner makes it easier to undo a tight bolt — the larger distance means a smaller force produces the same moment.

Gears are toothed wheels that transmit rotational motion and force. When two gears are meshed together, they turn in opposite directions. A large gear driving a small gear increases the speed of rotation but reduces the force. A small gear driving a large gear decreases the speed but increases the force (the turning moment).

Key Fact

Gears are force multipliers: a small gear driving a large gear increases the moment because the larger gear has a greater radius, so the force acts at a larger distance from the axle.

Momentum

Momentum is a property of all moving objects. It is calculated using:

$$p = m \times v$$

where \(p\) is momentum in kilogram metres per second (kg m/s), \(m\) is mass in kilograms (kg) and \(v\) is velocity in metres per second (m/s). Momentum is a vector quantity — it has both magnitude and direction.

In a closed system (where no external forces act), the total momentum before an event equals the total momentum after. This is the conservation of momentum. It applies to all collisions and explosions.

In a collision between two objects: \(m_1 v_1 + m_2 v_2 = m_1 v_1' + m_2 v_2'\). In an explosion where objects start at rest, the total momentum is zero before and after — so the objects move in opposite directions with equal and opposite momenta.

Force, Momentum and Safety

The force acting on an object is equal to the rate of change of momentum:

$$F = \frac{m \Delta v}{\Delta t}$$

This means that to reduce the force during a collision, you can increase the time over which the momentum changes. Car safety features exploit this principle: crumple zones deform slowly, increasing the collision time and reducing the force on passengers. Seat belts stretch slightly, air bags inflate to cushion impact, and cycle helmets contain foam that compresses on impact — all increasing the time of deceleration.

A 1200 kg car travelling at 15 m/s collides with a stationary 800 kg car. After the collision, they move off together. Calculate their shared velocity.

Total momentum before = \(1200 \times 15 + 800 \times 0 = 18{,}000\) kg m/s

Total momentum after = \((1200 + 800) \times v = 2000v\)

$$v = \frac{18{,}000}{2000} = 9 \text{ m/s}$$
lessons.exam_tip_html: In momentum calculations, always define a positive direction first. Objects moving in opposite directions have opposite signs for velocity. For moment questions, draw a diagram showing forces and distances from the pivot — this helps avoid errors with perpendicular distances.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The moment of a force is \(M = F \times d\); for equilibrium, total clockwise moments equal total anticlockwise moments (principle of moments).
  • Levers and gears are force multipliers that use moments to increase the output force from a smaller input force.
  • Momentum (\(p = mv\)) is conserved in a closed system; car safety features increase collision time to reduce force on passengers.

lessons.title: Reflection, Sound Waves and Waves for Detection
lessons.description: How sound and ultrasound waves are used for imaging and detection.
lessons.content_html:
Reflection of Waves

When a wave hits a boundary between two different materials, it can be reflected, absorbed or transmitted. The law of reflection states that the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection. Both angles are measured from the normal — an imaginary line drawn at right angles to the surface at the point of incidence.

Specular reflection occurs on smooth surfaces (like mirrors), where all the reflected rays are parallel, producing a clear image. Diffuse reflection occurs on rough surfaces, where the reflected rays scatter in many directions because the normal is different at every point on the surface. Most objects are seen by diffuse reflection of light.

Key Fact

The law of reflection applies to all waves (light, sound, water). The angle of incidence always equals the angle of reflection, measured from the normal to the surface.

Sound Waves

Sound waves are longitudinal waves produced by vibrating objects. They need a medium (solid, liquid or gas) to travel through — they cannot travel through a vacuum. In a sound wave, particles vibrate back and forth along the direction of energy transfer, creating regions of high pressure (compressions) and low pressure (rarefactions).

The speed of sound depends on the medium. Sound travels fastest in solids (about 5000 m/s in steel), slower in liquids (about 1500 m/s in water) and slowest in gases (about 340 m/s in air at room temperature). This is because particles are closer together in solids, so vibrations pass from one particle to the next more quickly.

The human ear can detect sounds with frequencies between approximately 20 Hz and 20,000 Hz (20 kHz). Sounds below 20 Hz are called infrasound, and sounds above 20 kHz are called ultrasound. The human hearing range decreases with age — older people typically cannot hear the highest frequencies.

The pitch of a sound depends on its frequency (higher frequency = higher pitch), while the loudness depends on its amplitude (greater amplitude = louder sound).

Ultrasound for Detection and Imaging

Ultrasound has many practical applications. In medical imaging, ultrasound waves are sent into the body. When they reach a boundary between two different tissues (for example, between fluid and solid tissue), some of the wave is reflected back. A computer analyses the reflected pulses to build an image of internal structures. This is commonly used for prenatal scans to monitor the development of a baby during pregnancy.

Key Fact

Ultrasound is preferred over X-rays for prenatal scans because it does not use ionising radiation, making it safer for the developing baby.

Ultrasound is also used in industry to detect cracks and flaws inside metal structures without cutting them open (non-destructive testing). A pulse of ultrasound is sent into the metal, and any internal crack or defect will reflect some of the wave back earlier than the far boundary, showing up on a display.

Echo sounding (sonar) uses ultrasound to measure the depth of water or locate objects underwater. A pulse of ultrasound is sent from a ship towards the seabed. The time taken for the echo to return is measured. The depth is calculated using:

$$\text{distance} = \frac{\text{speed} \times \text{time}}{2}$$

The division by 2 accounts for the fact that the pulse travels to the seabed and back. The same principle is used by bats and dolphins for echolocation — emitting ultrasound pulses and listening for reflections to navigate and find prey.

Seismic Waves for Detection

Seismic waves are produced by earthquakes and travel through the Earth. P-waves (primary waves) are longitudinal and travel through solids and liquids. S-waves (secondary waves) are transverse and can only travel through solids — they cannot pass through liquids. By analysing how seismic waves travel through the Earth, scientists have deduced the internal structure of the planet.

The fact that S-waves are not detected on the opposite side of the Earth from an earthquake (in the “shadow zone”) tells us that the Earth has a liquid outer core. P-waves are refracted as they pass through different layers, providing evidence for the density changes at the mantle-core boundary.

P-waves are longitudinal (particles vibrate parallel to the direction of travel), travel through solids and liquids, and are faster than S-waves — they arrive at seismometers first (hence “primary”). S-waves are transverse (particles vibrate perpendicular to the direction of travel), travel through solids only, and are slower (hence “secondary”). Both types are refracted when they pass between layers of different density.
lessons.exam_tip_html: In wave calculation questions, remember that for echo/sonar problems you must halve the total distance because the wave travels there and back. For seismic wave questions, link S-wave behaviour (cannot travel through liquids) to the evidence for a liquid outer core — this is a common 6-mark question topic.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection (measured from the normal); specular reflection gives clear images, diffuse reflection scatters light.
  • Sound waves are longitudinal, need a medium, and travel fastest in solids; ultrasound is used for medical imaging, industrial testing and sonar.
  • Seismic P-waves (longitudinal) pass through solids and liquids; S-waves (transverse) only pass through solids, providing evidence for Earth’s liquid outer core.

lessons.title: Lenses, Visible Light and Black Body Radiation
lessons.description: How lenses form images, colour filters work, and objects emit radiation.
lessons.content_html:
Convex and Concave Lenses

A convex lens (converging lens) is thicker in the middle than at the edges. It bends parallel rays of light inward so they meet at a single point called the principal focus (or focal point). The distance from the centre of the lens to the principal focus is called the focal length.

A concave lens (diverging lens) is thinner in the middle than at the edges. It spreads parallel rays of light outward so they appear to come from a single point behind the lens. Concave lenses always produce virtual, upright, diminished images.

Key Fact

A convex lens can produce real or virtual images depending on the position of the object. A concave lens always produces a virtual, upright, diminished image regardless of object position.

To draw a ray diagram for a convex lens, you need three standard rays from the top of the object: (1) a ray parallel to the principal axis, which refracts through the principal focus on the other side; (2) a ray through the centre of the lens, which passes straight through without bending; (3) a ray through the principal focus on the near side, which refracts to become parallel to the principal axis. Where the refracted rays meet is where the image forms.

If the object is beyond twice the focal length (\(> 2F\)), the image is real, inverted and diminished. At exactly \(2F\), the image is real, inverted and the same size. Between \(F\) and \(2F\), the image is real, inverted and magnified. Inside \(F\), the image is virtual, upright and magnified (this is how a magnifying glass works).

Magnification

The magnification produced by a lens tells you how much larger or smaller the image is compared to the object:

$$\text{magnification} = \frac{\text{image height}}{\text{object height}}$$

A magnification greater than 1 means the image is larger than the object. A magnification less than 1 means the image is smaller. Magnification has no units.

Visible Light and Colour

White light is a mixture of all the colours of the visible spectrum (red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet). When white light passes through a prism, each colour is refracted by a slightly different amount — violet is refracted the most and red the least — causing the light to spread into a spectrum. This is called dispersion.

Colour filters work by absorbing certain wavelengths and transmitting others. A red filter absorbs all colours except red, which it transmits. An opaque object appears a particular colour because it reflects that wavelength and absorbs all others. A red object in green light appears black because there is no red light to reflect.

The three primary colours of light are red, green and blue. Combining all three in equal proportions gives white light. Combining two primary colours gives a secondary colour: red + green = yellow, red + blue = magenta, green + blue = cyan. This is additive colour mixing and is used in TV and phone screens.

Colour filters and pigments use subtractive colour mixing. A cyan filter absorbs red and transmits blue and green. Placing a cyan filter and a yellow filter together absorbs both red and blue, transmitting only green.

Black Body Radiation

All objects emit and absorb thermal radiation (infrared radiation). The hotter an object, the more radiation it emits per second and the shorter the peak wavelength of the radiation. A black body is a theoretical object that absorbs all radiation that falls on it and emits a characteristic spectrum that depends only on its temperature.

Key Fact

As the temperature of a black body increases, the peak wavelength shifts towards shorter wavelengths (from infrared to red to white to blue). The total energy radiated per second also increases dramatically.

At room temperature, objects emit mainly infrared radiation (invisible). As they heat up, they begin to glow red (about 500°C), then orange, yellow and eventually white-hot at very high temperatures. Stars are approximate black bodies — a red star is cooler than a yellow star, which is cooler than a blue-white star.

The Earth absorbs short-wavelength radiation from the Sun (visible light and UV) and re-emits longer-wavelength infrared radiation. If the rate of absorption equals the rate of emission, the temperature remains stable. Greenhouse gases in the atmosphere absorb some of the outgoing infrared radiation and re-emit it back towards the Earth, increasing the surface temperature. This is the greenhouse effect — a natural process that makes Earth habitable, but increasing greenhouse gas concentrations are enhancing it, causing global warming.

For black body questions, remember: hotter = more radiation emitted AND shorter peak wavelength.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Convex lenses converge light and can form real or virtual images; concave lenses diverge light and always form virtual, diminished images.
  • White light disperses into a spectrum through a prism; colour filters absorb some wavelengths and transmit others.
  • All objects emit thermal radiation; hotter objects emit more radiation at shorter peak wavelengths, as described by the black body radiation curve.

lessons.title: Electromagnetic Induction and Transformers
lessons.description: How moving magnets generate electricity and how transformers work.
lessons.content_html:
Electromagnetic Induction

When a conductor moves through a magnetic field, or when a magnetic field changes around a conductor, a potential difference (voltage) is induced across the conductor. If the conductor is part of a complete circuit, a current flows. This process is called electromagnetic induction.

The induced potential difference can be increased by: moving the magnet (or conductor) faster, using a stronger magnet, or increasing the number of turns on the coil. Reversing the direction of movement or reversing the polarity of the magnet reverses the direction of the induced potential difference and current.

Key Fact

A potential difference is only induced while the magnetic field is changing. If the magnet is held stationary inside the coil, no potential difference is induced — there must be relative movement between the magnet and the conductor.

Fleming’s left-hand rule is used for the motor effect — when a current-carrying conductor is placed in a magnetic field and experiences a force. The thumb represents the direction of force (motion), the first finger represents the magnetic field, and the second finger represents the current.

Electromagnetic induction is essentially the reverse of the motor effect. Instead of a current causing motion, motion (or a changing field) causes a current. Generators work on this principle — a coil rotates in a magnetic field, inducing a continuously changing potential difference.

Generators: AC and DC

An alternator (AC generator) produces alternating current. A coil rotates between the poles of a magnet, and the induced potential difference reverses direction every half turn. This produces a sinusoidal (wave-shaped) output. The coil is connected to the external circuit via slip rings and brushes, which allow continuous rotation.

A dynamo (DC generator) uses a split-ring commutator instead of slip rings. The commutator swaps the connections every half turn, so the current always flows in the same direction in the external circuit, though it still varies in magnitude.

Key Fact

Increasing the speed of rotation or the strength of the magnet increases both the peak voltage and the frequency of the output from a generator.

Transformers

A transformer changes the voltage of an alternating current (AC) supply. It consists of two coils of wire (the primary and secondary) wrapped around a soft iron core. When AC flows through the primary coil, it creates a changing magnetic field in the iron core. This changing field induces a potential difference in the secondary coil.

The transformer equation relates the voltages and number of turns:

$$\frac{V_p}{V_s} = \frac{N_p}{N_s}$$

where \(V_p\) and \(V_s\) are the primary and secondary voltages, and \(N_p\) and \(N_s\) are the number of turns on the primary and secondary coils.

A step-up transformer has more turns on the secondary coil than the primary, so it increases the voltage. A step-down transformer has fewer turns on the secondary, so it decreases the voltage. In an ideal (100% efficient) transformer, electrical power is conserved:

$$V_p \times I_p = V_s \times I_s$$

This means that if the voltage is stepped up, the current is stepped down by the same factor, and vice versa. Real transformers are not perfectly efficient because some energy is lost as heat in the coils (due to resistance) and in the core (due to eddy currents and magnetisation/demagnetisation losses).

The National Grid

The National Grid transmits electricity from power stations to consumers across the country. Electricity is transmitted at very high voltages (up to 400,000 V) and correspondingly low currents. Since power lost as heat in the cables is given by \(P = I^2 R\), transmitting at low current greatly reduces energy losses.

Step-up transformers at power stations increase the voltage for efficient long-distance transmission. Step-down transformers near homes and businesses reduce the voltage to safe, usable levels (230 V for domestic supply in the UK).

Transformers require a continuously changing magnetic field to induce a voltage in the secondary coil. Direct current (DC) produces a constant magnetic field (after the initial switch-on), so no voltage is induced in the secondary coil. Alternating current continuously reverses direction, creating the constantly changing magnetic field needed for electromagnetic induction. This is a key reason why AC is used for mains electricity distribution.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Transformer calculations are common. Always write the equation first, then substitute. Check whether the transformer is step-up or step-down to verify your answer makes sense. For National Grid questions, always link high voltage to low current to reduced power loss using \(P = I^2 R\) — this three-step chain is what earns full marks.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Electromagnetic induction occurs when a conductor experiences a changing magnetic field, inducing a potential difference (and current in a complete circuit).
  • Transformers use electromagnetic induction to step voltage up or down; they only work with AC because a changing current is needed to create a changing magnetic field.
  • The National Grid uses high voltage (low current) transmission to reduce energy losses in cables, with step-up and step-down transformers at each end.

lessons.title: Space Physics: The Solar System and Beyond
lessons.description: Our solar system, life cycle of stars, and evidence for the Big Bang.
lessons.content_html:
Our Solar System

Our solar system consists of the Sun (a main sequence star), eight planets, dwarf planets (such as Pluto), moons, asteroids and comets. The four inner planets (Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars) are small, rocky and relatively close to the Sun. The four outer planets (Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune) are much larger gas giants, further from the Sun.

All planets orbit the Sun in roughly the same plane, in the same direction, in slightly elliptical orbits. The Sun contains over 99% of the mass of the solar system. Gravity provides the centripetal force needed to keep planets in orbit around the Sun, and moons in orbit around planets.

Key Fact

For a stable circular orbit, the gravitational force provides exactly the right centripetal force. A planet closer to the Sun orbits faster because the gravitational pull is stronger and the orbital radius is smaller.

Natural satellites (moons) orbit planets. Earth has one moon, while Jupiter has over 90 known moons. Asteroids are small, irregular rocky bodies that mostly orbit the Sun in the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter. Comets are bodies of ice and dust with highly elliptical orbits. When a comet approaches the Sun, it heats up and develops a glowing tail of gas and dust that always points away from the Sun (due to the solar wind).

The speed of a comet changes throughout its orbit. It moves fastest when closest to the Sun (perihelion) because the gravitational pull is strongest, and slowest when furthest from the Sun (aphelion).

The Life Cycle of Stars

All stars begin as a nebula — a large cloud of hydrogen gas and dust. Gravity causes the cloud to collapse and compress. As it contracts, it heats up. When the temperature at the core reaches about 15 million °C, hydrogen nuclei begin to fuse into helium — nuclear fusion begins and a star is born. The star enters its main sequence phase, where it spends most of its life.

During the main sequence, the outward pressure from nuclear fusion is balanced by the inward pull of gravity. This balance keeps the star stable. The Sun is currently in its main sequence phase and has been for about 4.6 billion years.

Key Fact

The fate of a star depends on its mass. Stars about the size of the Sun become red giants, then white dwarfs. Stars much more massive than the Sun become red supergiants, then explode as supernovae, leaving behind a neutron star or black hole.

Sun-sized stars: When hydrogen fuel runs low, the core contracts and the outer layers expand and cool, forming a red giant. The star then sheds its outer layers as a planetary nebula, leaving behind a dense, hot white dwarf that gradually cools over billions of years.

Massive stars: These swell into red supergiants, then collapse catastrophically in a supernova — an explosion so bright it can briefly outshine an entire galaxy. The remnant core may form a neutron star (incredibly dense, about 10 km across) or, if massive enough, a black hole. The elements created inside stars and scattered by supernovae form the raw materials for new stars, planets and even life.

Red-Shift and the Big Bang

When we observe light from distant galaxies, we find that the absorption lines in their spectra are shifted towards the red end of the spectrum compared to where we would expect them. This is called red-shift. It occurs because the galaxies are moving away from us, stretching the wavelength of the light. The further away a galaxy is, the greater its red-shift — meaning it is moving away faster. This relationship is known as Hubble’s Law.

The observation that all distant galaxies show red-shift (and that more distant galaxies show greater red-shift) is strong evidence that the universe is expanding. If we imagine reversing this expansion, all matter would converge to a single point. This leads to the Big Bang theory — the idea that the universe began from an extremely hot, dense point approximately 13.8 billion years ago and has been expanding ever since.

The cosmic microwave background radiation (CMBR) is low-energy microwave radiation that fills the entire universe in every direction. It was first detected in 1965 by Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson. The CMBR is the cooled remnant of the intense radiation released shortly after the Big Bang, now at a temperature of about 2.7 K (−270.5°C). Its existence provides strong supporting evidence for the Big Bang theory.

Together, red-shift and the CMBR provide two independent lines of evidence for the Big Bang. The discovery of the CMBR was predicted by Big Bang theory before it was detected — a successful prediction that greatly strengthened confidence in the theory.

Dark Matter and Dark Energy

Observations of galaxy rotation suggest that galaxies contain much more mass than we can see — stars at the edges of galaxies rotate faster than expected. Scientists propose that this “missing mass” is dark matter, which does not emit or absorb electromagnetic radiation but does exert gravitational effects. Observations also show that the expansion of the universe is accelerating. The unknown cause of this accelerating expansion is called dark energy. Together, dark matter and dark energy make up about 95% of the total mass-energy of the universe.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For star life cycle questions, draw a clear pathway and include all stages. The most common error is confusing the end stages — remember that only massive stars go supernova. For red-shift questions, link the three key ideas: distant galaxies show red-shift, which means they are moving away, which means the universe is expanding, which supports the Big Bang.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The solar system contains the Sun, eight planets, dwarf planets, moons, asteroids and comets, all held in orbit by gravity.
  • A star’s life cycle depends on its mass: Sun-sized stars end as white dwarfs, while massive stars explode as supernovae, leaving neutron stars or black holes.
  • Red-shift of distant galaxies and the cosmic microwave background radiation are the two key pieces of evidence that the universe began with a Big Bang and is still expanding.
